extracted.intended_audience: readers and policymakers interested in education, political economy, and institutional reform
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and prescriptive observations about what public and private education should teach, how institutions should be organized and funded, and what aims different parts of education ought to pursue. Focuses on curriculum content, institutional incentives, access for common people and women, and the social effects of the division of labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach logic before other sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: The student ought to understand well the difference between good and bad reasoning before he was led to reason upon subjects of so great importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logic (the science of general principles of good and bad reasoning) arose from examining arguments used to support philosophical systems; it was commonly taught prior to physics and ethics so students could distinguish probable from demonstrative arguments and avoid fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize experimental and observational sciences over metaphysical subtleties
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of experiment and observation (physics) was almost entirely neglected while metaphysics/pneumatics and ontology (doctrines concerning spirits and attributes common to mind and body) were overcultivated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphysics and ontology often produced subtleties and sophisms with little practical discovery; a sound curriculum should emphasize subjects where careful attention yields useful discoveries rather than cobweb subtleties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teaching philosophy primarily as subservient to theology
rubrics_metrics.description: When philosophy was taught only as subservient to theology, moral and natural philosophy were turned toward casuistry and ascetic morality (penance, mortification) rather than improving understanding or conduct in this life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching philosophy mainly to prepare for theology corrupted moral philosophy by focusing on rewards and punishments in a life to come rather than the perfection and happiness achievable in this life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum relevance: education should prepare for real business
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of what is taught in schools and universities does not seem to be the most proper preparation for the real business of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public education should teach what is useful for the occupations and social roles students will actually undertake; extravagant or disconnected parts of education waste the critical years before professional life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public institutions should adopt improvements and avoid sheltering obsolete systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Many universities have been slow to adopt modern improvements and have acted as sanctuaries for exploded systems and obsolete prejudices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richer, well-endowed universities are often slowest to change because their revenue is independent of teaching success; poorer institutions and private teachers, dependent on reputation, are more receptive to current opinions and improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of foreign travel for young people — avoid too early
rubrics_metrics.description: Sending young people to travel in foreign countries immediately upon leaving school (at 17–18) often makes them return conceited, dissipated, unprincipled, and incapable of serious application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travelling very young risks wasting formative years in frivolous dissipation away from parental control; travel later, after some maturity, may be more beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/gymnastic education to prepare citizens for military service
rubrics_metrics.description: Gymnastic exercises were intended to harden the body, sharpen courage, and prepare citizens for the fatigues and dangers of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Greek militia was notably effective, gymnastic education successfully achieved its intended military and civic purposes and should be part of public training where military readiness matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about music education's moral effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Music was proposed to humanize the mind and soften the temper, but comparison with Roman morals suggests musical education had little effect in mending morals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cautions against overrating musical education as a means to public morality: practical evidence suggests societies without formal musical instruction (Romans) had superior private and public morals compared to Greeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: State provision: public need not or should not directly pay all masters
rubrics_metrics.description: Masters who instructed young people in music or military exercises do not seem to have been paid or appointed by the state; the state provided the place of exercise but left students to find masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State can require citizens to be fit for service (e.g., in war) while leaving instruction to private masters; public provision of practice facilities (fields, training grounds) may suffice without directly employing teachers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial public payment to teachers preserves incentive and diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the schoolmaster were wholly or principally paid by the public, he would soon learn to neglect his business; partial public support with private fees keeps him attentive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mixed payment model (teacher partly paid by public, partly by fees) maintains incentives for teaching quality; wholly public-funded teachers risk negligence due to lack of dependence on reputation or fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid privileges/credential barriers that stifle private teachers
rubrics_metrics.description: Privileges of graduation and required attendance at public lectures create barriers: private teachers cannot compete and are regarded as the lowest order of men of letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When professional privileges and credentials are obtainable only through public institutions, private instruction is discouraged; this reduces competition and can corrupt the diligence of public teachers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public should ensure basic literacy and numeracy for the common people
rubrics_metrics.description: The most essential parts of education—to read, write, and account—can be acquired early and the public can facilitate acquisition by establishing parish or district schools where children may be taught for a moderate reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parish schools partly publicly supported (but not wholly paid) can make basic education affordable to common labourers; Scottish parish schools are held up as an effective model, English charity schools less universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as remedy to degeneracy caused by division of labour
rubrics_metrics.description: The division of labour confines most labourers to few simple operations, dulling their understandings, corrupting courage, and rendering them incapable of judging public interests or defending the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ordinary employments shape understanding, public attention to educating the common people is necessary in civilized and commercial societies to prevent intellectual and moral degeneration among the labouring poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women's education should be practical and focused on household roles
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no public institutions for the education of women; their education tends to useful purposes: improving natural attractions and forming the mind to reserve, modesty, chastity, and economy to make them fit mistresses of families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women's education, being privately directed, is narrowly tailored to the useful social roles they are expected to assume; the author presents this as appropriate given social expectations of the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of courts and legal education affects public morals and law quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Roman courts with single or few judges, practicing deliberation in public and sheltering themselves under precedent, led to orderly law and respect for oaths; Greek mob-like courts produced more random decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention to practice and precedent in judicial bodies forms a regular and orderly legal system; legal instruction and institutional design (small, accountable courts) should cultivate these practices.
